subject: physics
title: Required practical: measuring wave speed
key_idea: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. In a ripple tank, find the wavelength and frequency, or time a wave over a measured distance. The speed of sound is found by timing a sound over a known distance. For an echo, the sound travels there and back.

blocks.text: This section links the three quantities that describe a wave. Every measurement in this practical comes back to them.

items.meaning: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position.
The distance from a point on one wave to the same point on the next wave.
The number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one wave to pass a point.
How fast the wave moves through the medium, or how fast it transfers energy.

blocks.label: Wave equation
where: wave speed, v, in metres per second (m/s)

items.text: A ripple has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 3 cm. Change 3 cm to 0.03 m.
v = 0.15 m/s. The period is 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 s.

period = 1 ÷ frequency.

sections.heading: Measuring waves in a ripple tank

blocks.text: A ripple tank makes water waves. A lamp above it casts a shadow of the waves on a screen below, so the wave pattern can be seen and measured.

items: Place a metre rule against the screen, along the direction the waves travel.
Take a photograph of the shadow, or use a strobe light, so the waves are not moving.
Measure across several wavelengths, not just one.
Divide the distance by the number of wavelengths.
Count the number of waves passing a point in a measured time, using a stop clock.
Divide the number of waves by the time taken.
A signal generator or vibrating bar may also show the frequency.

blocks.label: Frequency from a count
blocks.formula: frequency = number of waves ÷ time taken

items: Measure the distance one wavefront travels, such as the length of the tank, with a metre rule.
Time it over that distance with a stopwatch.
Divide the distance by the time.
Or use wave speed = frequency × wavelength with the two values already found.

blocks.text: Test yourself with new numbers each time.

diagram.alt: Calculate the wave speed of a wave on a string from its frequency and wavelength.
diagram.question: A wave on a stretched string has a frequency of {f} Hz and a wavelength of {w} m. Calculate the wave speed.

items: Measure across many wavelengths and divide, to find the wavelength accurately.
Find the frequency by counting waves in a measured time.
Wave speed = distance ÷ time, or frequency × wavelength.

sections.heading: Measuring the speed of sound in air

blocks.text: Sound is too fast to time over a short distance, so the method needs a long distance and careful timing. There are two common methods.
Method 1: a starting pistol or clap

items: One student makes a sound, such as a starting pistol, cymbals or wooden blocks.
A second student stands a long way away and measures the distance with a tape measure or trundle wheel.
The second student starts a stopwatch on seeing the flash or smoke, and stops it on hearing the bang.
Divide the distance by the time.
Stand a measured distance from a large wall and make a sharp sound, such as banging two bricks together.
Time from the bang to the echo.
The sound travels to the wall and back, so the distance travelled is double the distance to the wall.
Or halve the time to the echo.

items.text: A wall is 85 m away. The sound travels there and back: 2 × 85 = 170 m.
The echo comes back after 0.50 s. Speed = 170 ÷ 0.50 = 340 m/s.

items: Repeat the timings and calculate a mean. Remove any anomalies.
Use a longer distance, so human reaction time is a smaller part of the time measured.
Waves on a string or spring can be measured too: use a vibration generator for a known frequency, measure the wavelength with a metre rule, then use the wave equation.
Speed = distance ÷ time.
For an echo, the sound travels twice the distance to the wall.
Repeat the readings and use a longer distance to improve the results.

checks.q: A wave on a string has a frequency of 8 Hz and a wavelength of 0.50 m. Calculate the wave speed.
Describe how a student could measure the speed of sound in air using an echo from a wall.
checks.a: Measure the distance to a large wall with a tape measure or trundle wheel. Make a loud sound. Time from the sound to the echo with a stopwatch. The distance travelled is twice the distance to the wall. Speed = distance ÷ time. Repeat and calculate a mean.

checks.q: Why measure the distance across ten wavelengths on the screen, instead of one?
checks.a: Measuring across more than one wavelength and dividing by the number of wavelengths gives a more accurate value of the wavelength.

worked_example.question:
The teacher wanted to determine the speed of water waves in a ripple tank. The teacher did not measure the wavelength of the wave.

Explain how the teacher could determine the speed of the wave.
answer_points: Measure the distance travelled by a wave using a metre rule (or measure the length of the ripple tank).
Measure the time taken for the wave to travel that distance with a timer or stopwatch.
Divide the distance by the time.
worked_example.tip: The third mark is only given if the first two are scored.

worked_example.question:
Ripples travel out from the centre of a small circular pond to its edge.

Describe how a student could determine the wave speed of the ripples.
answer_points: Find the relevant time, for example the time for a ripple to travel from the centre to the edge.
Measure the specified distance, for example the radius of the pond.
worked_example.tip: Using v = f × λ and counting waves in a measured time is also accepted.
